content: A sudden flash of insight - the subjective 'Aha!' experience when a problem's solution appears abruptly rather than through incremental progress - has a measurable neural signature. Work using EEG and fMRI on verbal puzzle-solving found that insight solutions are preceded by a brief burst of high-frequency gamma-band activity localized to the right anterior superior temporal gyrus, appearing roughly a third of a second before the participant reports the answer. This gamma burst is itself preceded by an increase in alpha-band activity over visual cortex, thought to reflect a brief inward shift of attention that reduces external visual distraction right before the solution surfaces. The broader theory is that insight involves unconscious restructuring of a problem representation - breaking an impasse caused by an initial, unhelpful framing - rather than a purely conscious, stepwise search through the same representation. This is also why incubation (setting a problem aside) sometimes helps: it can allow weaker, previously suppressed associations to become active once the dominant but unproductive framing is no longer being rehearsed.
note: Directly relevant to what curiosity should feel like from the inside, not just what it selects for.

content: Young children acquire the grammar of their native language with a speed and apparent ease that most adults never match learning a second language, and the leading explanations point to differences beyond just 'more practice.' Infants as young as eight months can track the statistical regularities of speech - which syllables reliably follow which - well enough to segment a stream of nonsense speech into word-like units after only a couple of minutes of exposure, suggesting powerful implicit statistical learning is active very early. Elissa Newport's 'less is more' hypothesis proposes a counterintuitive twist: young children's more limited working memory may actually help grammar learning, because it forces them to process and store smaller, simpler chunks of the input, which happen to align well with the hierarchical, componential structure of grammar; adults' larger working memory lets them analyze bigger chunks holistically, which can work against discovering that same structure. Separately, a sensitive period narrowing around puberty is well documented for accent and certain grammatical judgments, coinciding with reduced neuroplasticity, though how much of the adult disadvantage is neural versus attentional, motivational, or social remains genuinely debated.
note: A real example of learning capacity varying by developmental stage - relevant to how this project's own 'study' mechanism might need to change over a topic's lifecycle.

content: Not all school subjects draw on the same cognitive machinery, which helps explain why some people feel strong in one area and weak in another. Subjects like history and introductory biology lean heavily on declarative and episodic memory - accumulating and retrieving discrete facts, dates, and named structures - while math and physics lean more on fluid reasoning: holding several abstract relationships in working memory at once and manipulating them according to formal rules, often building hierarchically on earlier steps so a gap anywhere in the chain blocks everything built on top of it. This is part of why math anxiety and early gaps compound so much more visibly than gaps in fact-heavy subjects, where a missed unit doesn't usually block the next one. Individual differences in spatial reasoning ability correlate fairly consistently with math and physics performance, and personality/attitude factors matter too - Carol Dweck's growth-mindset research found that believing ability is improvable through effort, rather than fixed, predicts better recovery from setbacks in exactly these harder, more cumulative subjects. So 'being good at math' looks less like a fixed trait and more like an interaction between spatial/working-memory aptitude, how early foundational gaps were handled, and whether setbacks were interpreted as fixed limits or fixable gaps.
note: Bears on this project's own mastery-vs-transferability distinction - memorization-heavy vs reasoning-heavy domains may need different curiosity signals.

content: Two main families of theory explain what drives curiosity in humans. Berlyne's classic account treats curiosity as a response to properties of the stimulus itself - novelty, complexity, uncertainty, and conflict between expectation and observation all raise arousal in a way that motivates exploration until it's resolved. George Loewenstein's information-gap theory reframes curiosity as arising from a felt gap between what you know and what you want to know: noticing a specific, nameable gap in your own knowledge is itself aversive, like a mild itch, and exploring to close that gap is intrinsically rewarding independent of any external payoff, which is why people will read a whole article just to learn how it ends even when the answer has no practical use. More recent computational accounts (learning-progress and compression-progress theories) sharpen this further: curiosity tracks not how much is unknown but how fast prediction is currently improving, which is why both fully mastered and hopelessly incomprehensible material feel equally uninteresting, and the sweet spot sits at material that's just barely learnable right now. Curiosity also varies as a stable trait across individuals, correlating with openness to experience and predicting better learning outcomes independent of raw ability.
note: The closest thing to this project's own theoretical grounding (Oudeyer/Schmidhuber learning-progress framing, already cited in README.md) stated as a self-contained topic.

content: The idiom 'curiosity killed the cat' reflects a folk association between cats and exploratory boldness, but scientific study of curiosity specifically in cats is thin compared to species like corvids, primates, rats, and dogs, where deliberate novel-object and exploration paradigms are well established. What exists on cats mostly falls under research into feline temperament and exploratory behavior more broadly: cats show a fairly consistent bold-shy personality dimension, with bolder individuals approaching novel objects and environments faster and more persistently, and this trait shows meaningful stability across a cat's life and even some heritability. Neophobia (fear of novelty) and neophilia (attraction to novelty) coexist in the same animal and shift with context - a hungry or safe cat explores more readily than a stressed one, and early-life exposure to varied, safe novelty (a sensitive period in kittenhood analogous to socialization windows in other species) predicts more exploratory adult behavior. So there is real evidence that cats vary in something like trait curiosity/boldness and that it is shaped by early experience, but it has not been formalized and measured against a unified 'curiosity' construct the way it has in some other species.
note: A useful edge case: whether the framing that works for human curiosity even generalizes to animals with much weaker evidence bases.
